tagline: A hook isn't fire-and-forget — its **structured JSON return** re-enters the session and **steers** it.
summary: It's tempting to think a hook just **runs a script and its output is logged**. Increasingly, the opposite is true: a hook returns **structured JSON** that **re-enters the session** and changes what happens next. `SessionStart` can ask Claude to **re-scan skills** or **set the session title**. `Stop` and `SubagentStop` can return **additionalContext** to feed Claude more and **continue the turn**. A `MessageDisplay` hook can **transform or hide** assistant text as it's shown. The return value is a **channel back in**, not a log line.

sections.heading: Two channels out of a hook
body: Every hook has the obvious channel: an **exit code** that can **allow or block** the thing it fired on. That's the fire-and-forget model — run, succeed or veto, done.

The second channel is **structured JSON** on stdout. When a hook returns a recognized shape (often under `hookSpecificOutput`), Claude Code **reads it and acts on it**. The hook stops being a gate and becomes a **participant** in the turn.

sections.heading: What the return can do
body: **SessionStart** can return `reloadSkills: true` to **re-scan skill directories**, or set the **session title** via `hookSpecificOutput.sessionTitle` on startup and resume. **Stop** and **SubagentStop** can return `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` to **give Claude feedback** and keep the turn going instead of ending it.

A **MessageDisplay** hook reaches the rendering layer: it can **transform or hide** assistant message text as it is displayed. Each of these is a different **re-entry point** — startup, turn-end, and display — and each takes a different shape of return.

sections.heading: Why this changes how you write hooks
body: If you treat a hook as a script whose output vanishes, you'll **discard the most useful channel**. The return value is **load-bearing**: a malformed or empty return is a missed chance to inject context, rescan skills, retitle, or shape display.
Design a hook around its **return contract**, not just its side effects. The exit code says *whether*; the JSON says *what to do next*.

diagram.caption: A hook has two channels: an exit code (allow/block) and a **structured JSON return** that re-enters the session and steers it.

nodes.label: Lifecycle event fires
nodes.note: SessionStart, Stop, SubagentStop, MessageDisplay, and friends. Each is a **re-entry point** where a hook can speak back in.

nodes.label: Hook script runs
nodes.note: Your script executes with the event's payload on stdin. It can do work — and, crucially, it can **return something**.

nodes.label: Exit code only → logged
nodes.note: The fire-and-forget path: succeed or **block**, output logged, nothing else changes. This is the model people assume is the whole story.

nodes.label: Structured JSON returned
nodes.note: A recognized shape — `reloadSkills`, `sessionTitle`, `additionalContext`, hide/transform — under `hookSpecificOutput`. The second, richer channel.

nodes.label: Return value re-enters the session
nodes.note: Claude Code **reads** the JSON and applies it: feeding context back, rescanning skills, retitling, or reshaping display.

nodes.label: Session behavior changes
nodes.note: Skills re-scanned · title set · turn **continued** via additionalContext · message hidden or transformed. The hook **steered** the session, it didn't just observe it.

scenarios.title: The model people assume: **fire and forget**
scenarios.note: The hook runs, succeeds or blocks, and its output is logged. Real — but only half the surface, and the less powerful half.

scenarios.title: The hook **talks back** and steers the turn
scenarios.note: A Stop hook returns additionalContext; Claude reads it and keeps going. A SessionStart hook returns reloadSkills; the skill set is rescanned mid-session.

misconceptions.myth: A hook just runs a script — its output is logged and ignored.
misconceptions.reality: A hook can return **structured JSON** that Claude Code reads and acts on: rescanning skills, setting the title, injecting context, reshaping display.
misconceptions.why: Most shell tooling treats stdout as a log. Hooks treat a recognized return shape as **instructions**, which is easy to miss until you rely on it.

misconceptions.myth: A hook's only power is allow-or-block via its exit code.
misconceptions.reality: Beyond block/allow, the JSON return is a **data channel back into the session** — `additionalContext` to continue a turn, `reloadSkills`, `sessionTitle`, message transform/hide.
misconceptions.why: Permission-style hooks made the exit code the famous lever, so the richer return channel stays invisible until you read the newer events.

misconceptions.myth: Once a turn stops, a hook can't make Claude keep working.
misconceptions.reality: **Stop** and **SubagentStop** hooks can return `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` to give Claude feedback and **continue the turn**.
misconceptions.why: "Stop" sounds terminal. The hook fires *at* the stop, and its return can reopen the turn rather than just observing the end of it.
